1.pericope_label: Joshua gathers Israel at Shechem and rehearses the acts of God

schools.summary: Gill treats the summons as a second assembly of the same representatives, cites Abarbinel on why Joshua recalled them, and reads the taking of Abraham as a calling by grace; Calvin makes free adoption the hinge of the address, dismissing the Jewish legends that would give Abraham a piety of his own and reading the hornets as the miracle no man could claim.

Henry finds in Joshua's renewed strength a sign that no one's work for God is done till life is done, sees Abraham as a brand snatched from the burning and an instance of God justifying the ungodly, and dwells on the mercy that recorded Israel's crying rather than their murmuring at the sea.

Clarke states the Shechem-and-Shiloh difficulty at its sharpest and canvasses the Septuagint reading, Shuckford and Mede before settling it by the ark's portability, and reads Balak's war as prosecuted by curses and by Midian's women; Wesley gives the two purposes of the assembly and reckons how many of the elders had seen Egypt with their own eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch lay out the two-part structure of the address and trace its Exodus vocabulary back to the promise at Moses' call, and Ellicott glosses the flood as the river and takes the hornets literally.

debates: Whether the assembly stood before God at Shechem or at Shiloh, and whether the ark was brought to them
outliers: Calvin rejects the rabbinic accounts of Abraham breaking Terah's idols or refusing to worship the Chaldean fire, since the text leaves him under the same guilt as his fathers

14.pericope_label: Choose you this day whom ye will serve, and the people answer

schools.summary: Gill roots the fear of the Lord in a sense of his goodness, and Calvin faces the scandal of the offer head-on, arguing that Joshua speaks by the Spirit to expose a zeal that builds without a foundation, and that the people's unprompted answer is what makes the covenant binding.

Henry stages the verse as an election between Jehovah and the rival attractions of antiquity and good fellowship, holds that religion may safely be referred to any free thought, and presses Joshua's resolution for his household as a pattern of leading before requiring.

Clarke catalogues the Chaldean, Egyptian and Canaanite gods still kept among them and quotes Trapp on the multitude's readiness to turn with the stream; Wesley denies that any real liberty was offered, since the law of Moses bound both Joshua and the people, and explains why the older idols were the more dangerous.

Keil and Delitzsch ground the offer in the nature of true worship, which cannot be commanded into being, and hear the first commandment behind the people's reply; Ellicott glosses Jehovah as the covenant name, notes that Joshua's line ends with him, and judges the people's answer to have missed Joshua's point.

debates: Whether the offer of a choice was genuine, a rhetorical probation, or an insinuation that left no liberty at all
outliers: Ellicott reads the people's protest as a failure of understanding, where the other sources take it as sincere

19.pericope_label: Ye cannot serve the LORD, and the people bind themselves

schools.summary: Calvin defends the harshness as an obtestation meant to rouse a sluggish people rather than drive them off, confines the warning about forgiveness to gross apostasy, and reads the strange gods as inclinations rather than images, noting from Judges how soon the promise faded; Gill takes the threat as Joshua's jealousy over a people he knew to be prone.

Clarke canvasses and rejects a textual emendation that would soften the saying, turns the self-witness into the formula of conscience as witness, judge and executioner, and urges that reformation begin at once; Wesley reads the impossibility as moral rather than absolute and thinks images really were still kept.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the exchange as a legal transaction in which the people's own testimony would convict them, and prefer to read the strange gods as idols of the heart; Ellicott grounds the whole warning in Israel's habit of serving Jehovah alongside the gods of other nations, and observes that nothing was actually done in obedience to Joshua's command.

debates: Whether the strange gods to be put away were real images still kept or the inclination of the heart
outliers: Clarke reports an emendation reading 'ye shall not cease to serve' which he judges ingenious but unsupported by any manuscript

25.pericope_label: The covenant made, written in the book, and the great stone set up

schools.summary: Calvin identifies the statute and ordinance with the law of Moses rather than any new speech, explains the stone as a memorial for what lies forgotten in unopened books, and ends on the melancholy note that so solemn a covenant held for only a few years; Gill reads the dismissal as Joshua's final leave-taking.

Clarke glosses the idiom of cutting a covenant as alluding to sacrifice, places the writing in a blank column of the great law-roll, and grounds the stone's testimony in its permanence; Wesley makes the statute binding on posterity and explains the figure of a stone that hears.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the day as a renewal of Sinai on the model of Moses in Moab and refuse to identify the sanctuary at Shechem with the ark; Ellicott defines the covenant as one against tolerating idolatry and reads Joshua's writing as the second authorial signature in the Old Testament, evidence that Scripture was conceived as one book from the first.

debates: Whether the sanctuary of the Lord at Shechem means the ark brought there for the ceremony

29.pericope_label: The death and burial of Joshua, and Israel faithful while he lived

schools.summary: Calvin turns the title servant of the Lord against the generation that soon abandoned him, hears in the dating of Israel's fidelity a tacit announcement of its end, and generalises the pattern into a law of church history; Gill explains the burial custom and treats the Greek addition about the circumcision knives as unfounded.

Henry frames the chapter's close as triumphs ending in funerals, weighs Joshua's title against the same title given Moses, and collects the tradition of the quaking hill and Bishop Patrick's note that no days of mourning were kept.

Clarke dates the death soon after the assembly, reports Augustine's witness to the Greek addition about the stone knives, wonders at the absence of public mourning, and distinguishes the private idolatry that persisted from the public idolatry that did not.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why no successor was appointed and record that Joshua's labours held while his generation lived; Ellicott infers from the surviving elders that his death was comparatively early and likens the period to a primitive Church whose brevity matches that of the Roman one.

debates: Whether Joshua's death at a hundred and ten was a full age or a comparatively early one
outliers: Gill rejects as unfounded the Greek addition about the circumcision knives which Clarke reports with Augustine's support

32.pericope_label: The bones of Joseph buried at Shechem, and the death of Eleazar

schools.summary: Calvin weighs the choice of burial-place, sets a censure on the people's delay beside the mark of respect, corrects a confused name in Stephen's speech, and closes his commentary on burial as a symbol of the resurrection; Gill reconciles the two attributions of carrying up the bones and preserves the Samaritan Chronicle's account of Eleazar's end.

Wesley recalls Joseph's two-hundred-year-old charge and suggests the whole assembly was convened partly to bury him, making the chapter a funeral sermon and a farewell at once; Clarke dates the burial to the completed conquest, reports the long Septuagint addition, and argues from Caesar, Homer and Virgil that a continuation by another hand impugns nothing.

Ellicott names Eleazar and Joshua the Moses and Aaron of their period, notes that nothing personal survives of the counsellor at whose word Joshua went out and came in, explains the grant in Ephraim by the tabernacle at Shiloh, and judges that strict obedience largely died with them.

debates: When the bones of Joseph were actually buried, and whether the notice implies a rebuke of delay
